synthesis.body: A reported case count measures effort, not coverage, and an assertion that cannot fail is worse than a missing one because it reports confidence. One review of otherwise careful test code found four distinct shapes, all green, all unable to red: a helper that pre-filtered the very field the assertion then checked, so attribution could not fail for any input; two string literals defined in the test file compared to each other while the subject was never invoked; `assert X or <non-empty constant>`; and `len(dict) == len(set(dict))`, true by construction. Each looked like coverage and each cost maintenance. Two habits catch the class cheaply. Derive coverage mechanically instead of counting cases: an AST sweep for the subject's finding-emission sites, driven with a recording collector, found four unexercised branches sitting behind a growing case count. Then mutation-test any assertion you rely on — weaken the subject and confirm the test reds. See also the empty-set positive-control topic, the unstubbed-negative-case topic, and the source-substring-pin topic; they are three further members of the same family.

title: A case count is not coverage — four assertion shapes that cannot fail
